analysis.one_liner: Tightens funding rules for company pensions and raises federal insurance premiums to keep promised retirement checks paid.
analysis.headline: The Senate passed it 97–2 on November 16, 2005, but the House never took it up; the House's own pension bill (H.R.2830) became the Pension Protection Act of 2006, carrying most of the same provisions.
analysis.plain_summary: After several major airlines dumped their pension plans onto the federal pension insurer, this bill forced companies to put real money behind promised pensions: plans had to fund benefits fully over roughly seven years using market-based interest rates, underfunded plans were barred from increasing benefits or paying out lump sums, and premiums to the Pension Benefit Guaranty Corporation went up. It also gave workers the right to sell company stock in their 401(k)s, notice of investment blackout periods, and independent investment advice, and it gave legal cover to 'cash balance' pension conversions and special funding relief to airlines that freeze benefits. The Senate passed it nearly unanimously; the House wrote its own version instead, which became the law.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers and retirees in company pension plans, who get stronger guarantees that promised benefits will actually be there; the federal Pension Benefit Guaranty Corporation, whose finances improve through higher premiums; and participants in 401(k)-style plans, who gain the right to diversify out of employer stock and get independent investment advice.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Pension participants and the federal pension insurer

how_it_helps.text: Requires single-employer pension plans to fully fund benefits already earned, phasing in over three years (five for small plans), and to amortize shortfalls over at most seven years [S3].
Bars benefit increases when a plan is less than 80% funded, and bars lump-sum payouts and benefit accruals when funding falls below 60%, protecting the plan's assets for promised benefits [S3].
Raises PBGC premiums, including a $30-per-participant flat premium in 2006, to strengthen the federal pension insurance fund [S3].

Requires 401(k)-type plans to let employees sell employer stock and choose at least three other investment options, with notice of blackout periods and periodic benefit statements — a response to Enron-type losses [S3].
Requires plans to give participants independent investment advice and investment education [S3].
Improves disclosure: funding notices to participants, financial information for multiemployer plans on request, and electronic posting of annual reports [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employers that sponsor traditional pension plans — especially weakly funded ones and airlines — face higher required contributions, steeper PBGC premiums, and restrictions on improving or paying out benefits; workers in deeply underfunded plans may see benefit accruals frozen; taxpayers back the PBGC if funding discipline still fails.

drawbacks.text: Stricter funding requirements raise employer costs sharply, which can push companies to freeze or terminate traditional pensions rather than fund them — accelerating the shift of retirement risk onto workers [S3].

The bill effectively legitimizes cash balance conversions: plans can be deemed age-discrimination-free if they follow the new rules, prospective application of conversion rules means older workers whose accruals were slowed in past conversions get no remedy from this law [S3].
Airlines that stop benefit accruals get special PBGC premium treatment, easing the cost burden on an industry that had just transferred large pension obligations to the federal insurer [S3].
The 'at-risk' funding rules key off corporate bond ratings, so the accuracy of required contributions depends on credit rating agencies' judgments [S3].
Limits on benefit increases and lump sums for weak plans, while protecting plan assets, can strand current workers' benefit growth for years [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is real: forcing companies to pre-fund pensions makes promised benefits far more secure and reduces the chance that the federal insurer — and ultimately taxpayers — absorbs the losses, which is what happened with the airlines. The cost is that pensions become more expensive for employers, encouraging freezes and conversions to cheaper plans, and the bill's blessing of cash balance conversions means many older workers' slower benefit accruals stand. On balance the funding discipline and participant protections outweigh the employer-relief carve-outs, but the airline premium relief and cash balance title show concentrated interests were accommodated.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate passed it 97–2 within about seven weeks of introduction, but the House never voted on the Senate bill — it passed its own pension bill, H.R.2830, which became the Pension Protection Act of 2006 carrying most of the same ideas.

narrative.text: Introduced September 28, 2005, and placed directly on the Senate Calendar the same day [S6].
Considered and passed the Senate with an amendment on November 16, 2005, by a vote of 97–2 — 55 of 55 Republicans, 41 of 44 Democrats, and the 1 Independent voted yes [S6][S7].
The Senate's action was sent to the House in December 2005, and the Senate's action history notes the companion measure H.R.2830; no House vote on S.1783 occurred before the Congress ended [S6].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Pension participants ultimately gained stronger funding rules when the House's version became the 2006 law; airlines freezing their plans and sponsors of cash balance conversions kept their favorable treatment either way.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Participants gained via the 2006 successor law

sides.party_line_note: Final passage was 97–2, with both parties nearly unanimous: all 55 Republicans, 41 of 44 Democrats, and the sole Independent voted yes [S7].

industries.note: The bill imposes special funding rules but also gives commercial airlines that freeze benefit accruals special PBGC premium treatment [S3]. Airlines had recently shifted massive pension obligations onto the federal insurer, so relief for freezes shifts risk to the public backstop.

industries.industry: Sponsors of traditional defined benefit pension plans
industries.note: Employers must fully fund earned benefits on shorter schedules, pay higher PBGC premiums, and lose flexibility to boost or cash out benefits when underfunded [S3]. That cost is what buys security for workers' pensions.

industries.industry: Sponsors of cash balance and other hybrid plans
industries.note: Title VI deems compliant hybrid plans nondiscriminatory as to age, ending legal uncertainty that had threatened cash balance conversions — conversions that slow older workers' benefit accruals [S3].
Higher flat and risk-based premiums plus tighter funding standards shore up the agency that guarantees pensions when employers fail [S3].
The bill limits the tax exclusion for death benefits under employer-owned life insurance and requires employer notice and employee consent before insuring an employee's life [S3].
Plans must provide independent investment advice and education to participants, creating a market for advisory services while giving workers professional guidance [S3].
